result: The authors generated quantitative 3D models of excitatory synaptic boutons in Layer 1 of human temporal lobe neocortex using transmission electron microscopy and 3D reconstructions from neocortical biopsy tissue obtained during epilepsy surgery. A total of 361 synaptic boutons were reconstructed from four patients (190 SBs and 184 AZs in L1a; 171 SBs and 165 AZs in L1b). The tissue was obtained from patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, with the epileptic focus in the hippocampus but not in the neocortical access regions, and the authors argue this tissue can be regarded as non-epileptic.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the quality and validity of the methodology. Reviewer 1 states the 'quantitative assessment of various synaptic parameters...is based on convincing experimental approaches.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the techniques used to obtain the data, as well as the analyses and the statistics performed by the Authors are all solid.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the work appears to be generally well done, the EM and EM tomography images are of very good quality. The analyses is clear and precise.' No concerns were raised about the tissue source or methodology.

result: The study found that excitatory synaptic boutons in L1 were medium-sized (mean surface area 5.48±1.40 µm², mean volume 0.50±0.19 µm³), comparable to L5 and L6 but ~2-fold larger than L4. The majority contained numerous mitochondria comprising ~7% of total volume (0.04±0.02 µm³ in L1a; 0.05±0.01 µm³ in L1b), with good correlation between SB volume and mitochondrial volume (R²: 0.7528 for L1a; R²: 0.5992 for L1b). SBs were predominantly located on dendritic spines (~80%).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these structural findings. Reviewer 1 states the study provides 'important information on the ultrastructural organization of layer 1' with 'convincing experimental approaches.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'the abundant and very precious data about the fine structure of the human neocortical layer 1' and that 'quantitative electron microscopy data...are very valuable.' No concerns were raised about these measurements.

result: The majority (~98%) of synaptic boutons in L1 had only a single active zone. PreAZs were on average 0.18±0.08 µm² in L1a and 0.22±0.04 µm² in L1b, with PSDs of similar size (0.21±0.01 µm² in L1a; 0.22±0.05 µm² in L1b). The majority of AZs (~80%) were macular and non-perforated. The average AZ surface area was ~0.20 µm², approximately 2- to 3-fold larger than in mouse and non-human primate neocortex. Only a weak correlation was found between SB surface area and PreAZ surface area.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the quality of the active zone measurements. Reviewer 2 states 'the techniques used to obtain the data, as well as the analyses and the statistics performed by the Authors are all solid, strengthen this manuscript, and support the conclusions drawn in the discussion.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the EM and EM tomography images are of very good quality. The analyses is clear and precise.' No concerns were raised about these structural parameters.

result: Excitatory SBs in L1 had a total pool of ~3500 SVs (L1a: 2958.62±1940.51; L1b: 3903.32±1852.23, significantly larger in L1b by ~1.3-fold), with a readily releasable pool of ~4 SVs (L1a: 5.90±5.05; L1b: 1.29±1.87 at p10 nm), recycling pool of ~470 SVs, and resting pool of ~2900 SVs (L1a: 2515.02±1588.99; L1b: 3277.97±1480.96). SVs had an average diameter of 25.03±5.27 nm (30.29±4.67 nm by TEM tomography). On average, 3.71±1.38 docked SVs were found in L1a and 3.42±1.34 in L1b. The total pool was larger than in other layers of human TLN (~2-fold vs L4, ~2.6-fold vs L5, ~3-fold vs L6).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the vesicle pool quantification. Reviewer 2 notes the study examined 'the number of the synaptic and the dense core vesicles, also differentiating between the readily releasable, the recycling and the resting pool of synaptic vesicles' and that 'the techniques used to obtain the data, as well as the analyses and the statistics performed by the Authors are all solid.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the work appears to be generally well done' with 'very good quality' images and 'clear and precise' analyses.

result: Astrocytic processes in L1 contributed ~20% to the total volume of the human temporal lobe neocortex, similar to L6 but much lower than L4 (~70-80%). In L1, the majority of spine and shaft synapses were not (~70%) or only partially (~20%) covered by fine astrocytic processes. Only ~10% of synapses in L1 showed fine astrocytic processes forming a 'tripartite' synapse, compared to much higher numbers in L4 (spines: ~50%; shafts: ~20%). Significant layer-specific differences exist in astrocytic coverage of synaptic complexes.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the astrocytic coverage findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the quantitative assessment of various synaptic parameters, astrocytic coverage and mitochondrial morphology is based on convincing experimental approaches.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the coverage of the synapse by astrocytic processes was also assessed' and that the analyses are 'solid.' No concerns were raised about these measurements or their interpretation.

result: The low degree of astrocytic coverage of L1 synaptic boutons suggests that glutamate spillover and synaptic crosstalk may occur at most synaptic complexes in L1, or alternatively that astrocytic processes remove spilled glutamate.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the Authors conclude that the subcellular morphology of the layer 1 synapses is suitable for the functions of the neocortical layer, i.e. the synaptic integration within the cortical column. The low glial coverage of the synapses might allow the glutamate spillover from the synapses enhancing synaptic crosstalk within this cortical layer' and affirms that the conclusions are 'support[ed]' by the data. No concerns were raised about this functional interpretation.

result: Layer 1 in the adult human neocortex can be subdivided into two sublaminae (L1a and L1b). L1a is dominated by a dense network of astrocytes, reactive microglia, and terminal tuft dendrites. Lipofuscin granules were frequently noted in astrocytes, microglia, and L1 neurons. A persistent subpopulation of excitatory Cajal-Retzius cells was found in humans (in contrast to rodents), and GABAergic interneurons constitute the predominant class of neurons in L1. The majority of synaptic complexes were axo-spinous (~80%), predominantly on mushroom spines (L1a: ~83%; L1b: ~73%), with ~90% of spines containing a spine apparatus.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these cellular and structural observations. Reviewer 1 notes the study provides 'new information on the detailed morphology of human neocortical tissue.' Reviewer 3 states 'the MS is well written easy to read. Result section gives a detailed set of figures showing many morphological parameters of synaptic boutons and surrounding glial elements' and that 'the work appears to be generally well done.' No concerns were raised about these descriptive findings.

result: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1 was relatively high (5.26×10⁸±8.44×10⁷ synapses/mm³ overall; L1a: 5.52×10⁸±1.25×10⁸; L1b: 5.01×10⁸±1.40×10⁷), indicating a relatively robust and strong connectivity of neurons within L1 of the human temporal lobe neocortex.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the synaptic density measurements and interpretation. Reviewer 1 states the 'quantitative assessment of various synaptic parameters...is based on convincing experimental approaches.' Reviewer 2 affirms the 'techniques used to obtain the data, as well as the analyses and the statistics performed by the Authors are all solid, strengthen this manuscript, and support the conclusions drawn in the discussion.' No concerns were raised about these density measurements or their functional interpretation.

result: The quantitative 3D models of excitatory synaptic boutons showed significant layer-specific differences in structural and synaptic parameters, particularly in the size of active zones and the total pool of synaptic vesicles, the putative RRP, RP, and resting pool compared to other previously studied layers (L4, L5, L6).
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the comparative findings across layers. Reviewer 2 notes 'all the above parameters were compared to other layers of the human temporal neocortex' and that 'the authors provide comparative data of all the layers examined by them so far in the Discussion.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'the manuscript is a follow-on study with 3 previous publications from the same authors on different layers of the temporal cortex' and that the comparative approach is valid. No concerns were raised about the layer-specific differences.

result: Background claims about Layer 1 anatomy, function, and the knowledge gap regarding its synaptic organization in humans. These include established facts about L1 receiving cortico-cortical projections, being the termination zone of tufted dendrites, its role in Ca²⁺ spike initiation, its conservation across species, its function as the predominant input layer for top-down information, and its role in attention, memory, and plasticity. The temporal lobe neocortex encompasses ~20% of the cerebral cortex and serves as the epicenter for temporal lobe epilepsy.
evaluation: These are background claims cited from established literature that reviewers do not question. Reviewer 1 notes the study provides 'important information' that 'will be of interest to neuroscientists working on different network functions,' implicitly accepting the functional context. Reviewer 3 states 'given that anatomical data in human brain are still very limited, the current MS has substantial relevance,' affirming the knowledge gap motivating the study. No concerns were raised about the background or contextual claims.
